1422436320874483715.a: I managed equipment in data centers for years. It was not unusual for a 10,000 Amp circuit to blow a panel 100ft across a room, knock a hole in the opposite wall, and set the room on fire. This usually happened while switching a large battery bank. Facility was designed for this.

1422437257777140842.a: The worst I have seen was a data center trying to power multiple huge battery backups from a single diesel locomotive. The load imbalance of switching a bunch of megawatt sized loads over to a single field coil on a generator is no joke. Grids are generators with ~infinite power.

1422440299742253081.a: For those counting, a diesel locomotive generates 4.5 Megawatts. It starts with no load. When you start adding loads to it the generator voltage starts swinging as the field coil collapses briefly under the strain. That's enough energy to make a person vaporize. Nevermind metal.

1422441367763046405.a: This is precisely why you see a field of power packs. The more generators you have the easier it is to balance the loads. It also provides redundancy and if done well isolation so the facility can still operate while actively on fire.

1422574039558668294.a: I'm like 90% certain these are from the food industry. Which is fine, toaster ovens have been used in the past for reflow. This is infinitely better because it has infrared heaters. The temperature needs to climb quickly, peak, and drop quickly before the FR4 PCB catches fire.

1422574040728932352.a: Ironically, FR4 means the resin binder is self extinguishing flame resistance level 4. It will sure as hell burn even if it doesn't flame up, though. And that will ruin your day.

1422575584295755777.a: I worked in electronics repair in college. It was very common to find large charcoal ringed holes burned through early, 70s-80s, PCBs from load resistors or vacuum tubes sitting next to the PCB. To their credit, the device often only failed when the parts fell out.
